lead: Some first order equations do not separate in x and y, but separate in the ratio y/x. Call such an equation homogeneous: the right side depends on x and y only through y/x. Writing v = y/x turns it into a separable equation in v and x. After a shift of origin, the same trick handles right sides that are a ratio of two linear expressions in x and y.
prereq: You need 1.1 for classifying the equation, and 1.2, because the substitution ends in a separable equation.

blocks.text: A function f(x, y) is homogeneous of degree n when f(λx, λy) = λⁿf(x, y) for every λ > 0. Here λ is a positive scaling factor and n is a fixed number, not necessarily a whole number.

items: x² + xy: degree 2, since (λx)² + (λx)(λy) = λ²(x² + xy).
1/(x + y): degree −1, since 1/(λx + λy) = λ⁻¹/(x + y).
x² + y: not homogeneous; it gives λ²x² + λy, not a single power of λ times the original.

blocks.text: A first order equation M dx + N dy = 0 is homogeneous when M and N are homogeneous of the same degree n. Then M/N is homogeneous of degree 0, so it depends only on y/x. Writing f(y/x) = −M/N gives dy/dx = f(y/x).
M dx + N dy = 0 is homogeneous ⟺ dy/dx = f(y/x)
blocks.where: M and N are functions of x and y, both homogeneous of the same degree n; f is a function of the single ratio y/x.

blocks.text: Quick test: replace x by λx and y by λy on the right side. If every λ cancels, the equation is homogeneous and the substitution below applies.
Set v = y/x, that is y = vx. Here v is a new unknown function of x. Differentiate y = vx by the product rule, remembering that v changes with x.
y = vx  ⟹  dy/dx = v + x dv/dx
blocks.where: v = y/x is the new dependent variable, y is the original dependent variable, x is the independent variable.

items: Check that the right side is homogeneous and write it as dy/dx = f(y/x).
Put y = vx and dy/dx = v + x dv/dx.
Substitute and cancel v: x dv/dx = f(v) − v.
Integrate both sides and keep one arbitrary constant C.
Replace v by y/x and simplify.
Apply any initial condition to fix C.

blocks.text: Step 3 makes the equation separable; 1.2 finishes it. Step 4 divides by f(v) − v, so every root v₀ of f(v) = v gives a possible straight line y = v₀x. Test those roots separately in the original equation.

Polar coordinates often tidy the answer. Put x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ, where r is distance from the origin and θ is angle from the x-axis. Then y/x = tan θ and x² + y² = r², so inverse tangents of y/x become plain θ.
The shape dy/dx = (a₁x + b₁y + c₁)/(a₂x + b₂y + c₂) is not homogeneous when any c is nonzero. Here a₁, b₁, c₁, a₂, b₂, c₂ are constants. Two cases are decided by a₁b₂ − a₂b₁.

items: Case a₁b₂ ≠ a₂b₁: the lines a₁x + b₁y + c₁ = 0 and a₂x + b₂y + c₂ = 0 meet at one point (h, k). Shift the origin with X = x − h and Y = y − k, where h and k solve a₁h + b₁k + c₁ = 0 and a₂h + b₂k + c₂ = 0. The equation becomes dY/dX = (a₁X + b₁Y)/(a₂X + b₂Y), which is homogeneous. Solve with v = Y/X and put X, Y back.
Case a₁b₂ = a₂b₁: the lines are parallel or identical, so no (h, k) exists. Put v = a₁x + b₁y. Then dv/dx = a₁ + b₁ dy/dx, and the equation separates in v and x.

blocks.text: Worked case a₁b₂ = a₂b₁: dy/dx = (2x + 3y − 1)/(4x + 6y − 5). Here 2·6 = 12 = 4·3, so the shift fails. With v = 2x + 3y, dv/dx = 2 + 3(v − 1)/(2v − 5) = (7v − 13)/(2v − 5), hence (2v − 5)dv/(7v − 13) = dx. Integrating gives (2/7)v − (9/49)ln|7v − 13| = x + C, and v = 2x + 3y finishes it.
Worked case a₁b₂ ≠ a₂b₁: dy/dx = (x + y + 1)/(x − y + 3). Solving h + k + 1 = 0 and h − k + 3 = 0 gives h = −2, k = 1. Then dY/dX = (X + Y)/(X − Y), the equation solved in the example below.

examples.question: Solve dy/dx = (x + y)/(x − y) with y = 0 when x = 1. Give the solution in polar form and find y at x = 0.5.
steps: The right side is (x + y)/(x − y). Numerator and denominator are homogeneous of degree 1, so the equation is homogeneous.
Put y = vx, so dy/dx = v + x dv/dx.
Then v + x dv/dx = (1 + v)/(1 − v).
Subtract v: x dv/dx = (1 + v²)/(1 − v).
Integrate: tan⁻¹v − ½ln(1 + v²) = ln|x| + C.
Put v = y/x. Since 1 + y²/x² = (x² + y²)/x², this becomes tan⁻¹(y/x) = ½ln(x² + y²) + C.
Apply y = 0 at x = 1: tan⁻¹0 = ½ln 1 + C, so C = 0. Thus tan⁻¹(y/x) = ½ln(x² + y²).
In polar form, y/x = tan θ and x² + y² = r², so θ = ln r, that is r = e^θ.
At x = 0.5, e^θ cos θ = 0.5. Solving gives θ ≈ 1.4537 rad, r ≈ 4.279, and y = r sin θ ≈ 4.249.
examples.answer: The solution is tan⁻¹(y/x) = ½ln(x² + y²), equivalently θ = ln r with r = e^θ, and y ≈ 4.249 when x = 0.5.

traps: For y = vx, dy/dx = v + x dv/dx. Writing only x dv/dx drops v and gives a wrong integral.
M and N must have the same degree. M = x² + y, N = xy looks homogeneous but mixes degrees 2 and 1; the substitution then fails.
Dividing by f(v) − v can lose lines y = v₀x where f(v₀) = v₀. Test those roots in the original equation.
In the linear-ratio form, compute a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ before shifting. If it is zero, the lines never meet and no (h, k) exists.
Finish by replacing v with y/x. An answer left in v has not solved the equation in x and y.

quiz.q: Define a homogeneous function of degree n and give one example of degree 2 and one function that is not homogeneous.
quiz.a: f is homogeneous of degree n when f(λx, λy) = λⁿf(x, y) for every λ > 0. Degree 2 example: x² + 3xy. Not homogeneous: x² + y.

quiz.q: Why does y = vx reduce a homogeneous equation to a separable one?
quiz.a: For M, N homogeneous of the same degree, M/N is homogeneous of degree 0, so it depends only on y/x = v. Substitution gives x dv/dx = f(v) − v, which separates as dv/(f(v) − v) = dx/x.
f(v) = v + tan v, so x dv/dx = tan v. Then cot v dv = dx/x, giving ln|sin v| = ln|x| + C, that is sin(y/x) = Cx.
With y = vx: v + x dv/dx = (1 + v²)/v, so x dv/dx = 1/v. Then v dv = dx/x, giving v²/2 = ln|x| + C, so y² = x²(2ln|x| + C′).

quiz.q: For dy/dx = (2x + 3y − 1)/(4x + 6y − 5), explain why the shift of origin cannot be used, then solve it.
quiz.a: Here 2·6 = 12 = 4·3, so the lines are parallel and no (h, k) exists. Put v = 2x + 3y: dv/dx = 2 + 3(v − 1)/(2v − 5) = (7v − 13)/(2v − 5). Separate to (2v − 5)dv/(7v − 13) = dx and integrate: (2/7)v − (9/49)ln|7v − 13| = x + C, with v = 2x + 3y.

quiz.q: A student solves dy/dx = (x + y)/(x − y) by v = y/x and divides by 1 + v². Which solutions could be lost, and is any genuine solution lost here?
quiz.a: Losses can come from roots of f(v) − v = 0 and from points where the original equation is undefined. Here f(v) − v = (1 + v²)/(1 − v), which has no real root; v = 1 means y = x, where the original denominator is zero, so it is not a solution. Nothing genuine is lost.

quiz.q: Which substitution handles dy/dx = (a₁x + b₁y + c₁)/(a₂x + b₂y + c₂) when a₁b₂ = a₂b₁?
quiz.a: v = a₁x + b₁y (or v = a₂x + b₂y). Then dv/dx = a₁ + b₁ dy/dx and the equation separates in v and x.

beyond: Not for the exam. Homogeneous functions obey Euler's theorem: if f is homogeneous of degree n, then x ∂f/∂x + y ∂f/∂y = n f(x, y). Economists use it to test returns to scale in Cobb–Douglas production functions. In fluid mechanics and heat transfer, similarity solutions assume a quantity depends only on a ratio of variables, the homogeneous substitution in disguise, turning a partial differential equation into an ordinary one.
